questions.q: What is the primary physical setting where the narrator first hears the 'लोज' (sound), and what time of day does it occur?
questions.a: The primary physical setting is the narrator's private study/room (ड्योढ़ी/कमरा) and it occurs at night (रात) when he is trying to sleep. A wrong answer (e.g., "art gallery" or "daytime") reveals the student has not distinguished the frame narrative (personal experience) from the essay's broader subject (art history), confusing the metaphorical setting with the literal one.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the 'atmosphere' of the opening paragraph differs from the atmosphere of the paragraph where the author discusses Raja Ravi Varma's prints reaching every home.
questions.a: The opening atmosphere is intimate, suspenseful, and subjective—dominated by the narrator's sensory confusion (डर, विस्मय, नींद टूटना) in a dark room. The later atmosphere becomes analytical, historical, and collective—discussing mass reproduction, public taste, and cultural shift with a tone of critical observation. A wrong answer that describes both as "sad" or "informative" shows the student cannot track tonal shifts across discourse modes (personal narrative vs. cultural criticism).

questions.q: The author writes: "लोज के कारण चित्रकला की फोटोग्राफी द्वारा सुरक्षा हुई है" (Due to sound, painting was protected by photography). Apply the concept of 'setting as argument' to explain why the author places this claim in the middle of a personal night-time experience rather than at the start of an art-history essay.
questions.a: Step 1: Identify the claim—photography 'saved' painting by fixing its fleeting oral context. Step 2: Locate the setting—this claim appears after the narrator's personal encounter with the gramophone record (लोज) in his room. Step 3: Connect—the private room (where sound invades silence) mirrors the public art world (where mechanical reproduction invades tradition). Step 4: Conclude—the domestic setting makes the abstract historical argument tangible: just as the narrator cannot escape the record's sound in his bedroom, traditional art could not escape photography's reach in Indian homes. A wrong answer that treats the claim as mere factual information misses how setting structures the essay's logic.

questions.q: Compare the 'setting' of the traditional artist's workspace (as described in the essay) with the 'setting' of the modern photo-studio. How does this spatial contrast construct the essay's central atmosphere of irreversible loss?
questions.a: The traditional workspace is implied through references to गुरु-शिष्य परम्परा, मौखिक निर्देश, and the artist's intimate engagement with the subject (e.g., Ravi Varma's early studio in Travancore). The modern photo-studio is explicitly described as a place where "तीन-चौथाई तीन आने के चित्र" are mass-produced, with no oral instruction, only mechanical repetition. The atmosphere of loss is constructed by the spatial replacement of the slow, sacred, sound-filled atelier by the fast, silent, commercial studio. A wrong answer listing only physical objects (easel vs. camera) fails to see that the essay uses space to embody the epistemological shift from श्रव्य to दृश्य.

questions.q: Evaluate the author's decision to end the essay with the image of "रात के तीन-तीन पहर" (three watches of the night) and the continuing sound of the record. Does this circular return to the opening setting strengthen or weaken the essay's argument about the permanence of mechanical reproduction? Justify.
questions.a: It strengthens the argument. The circular structure traps the reader in the same inescapable soundscape that traps the narrator—mechanical reproduction (the record) continues playing long after the human voice (tradition) has stopped. The night setting (darkness, insomnia, repetition) becomes a metaphor for a culture that cannot 'switch off' the mechanical age. A wrong answer calling it "just a nice ending" misses the structural irony: the essay begins with sound disturbing silence and ends with sound persisting into dawn, proving the author's thesis that फोटोग्राफी/लोज has permanently altered the Indian artistic soundscape.

questions.q: Write a 100-word diary entry from the perspective of a traditional court painter in 1890 who has just seen his first Ravi Varma oleograph in the palace. Use the essay's atmosphere of 'helpless fascination' to convey the setting of a dying art world.
questions.a: A strong entry will: (a) locate the painter in a specific physical space (palace workshop, dim lamp), (b) include sensory details from the essay (smell of turpentine vs. printed ink, silence of the print vs. chanted shlokas), (c) express the emotional atmosphere—admiration for the print's reach mixed with dread for his own obsolescence, (d) echo the essay's key terms (लोज, श्रव्य, दृश्य, प्रतिलिपि). A weak entry will be generic ("I am sad") without anchoring in the essay's specific historical setting or its unique atmosphere of intellectual complicity (the painter knows the print is 'better' for the public).
